title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 58 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 422–425 (Night 58, continuing directly from nights-57), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 58 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The merchant who has bought Nuzhat al-Zamān dresses her and takes her jewellery, hoping she will win him a royal letter from the governor of Damascus; learning that she knows King ʿUmar, he asks her to write him a letter to the king. She lists her learning, then writes verses of longing and a letter signed with her name. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-khamsūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and fifty,
sentences.i: And when it was the fifty-eighth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ التَّاجِرَ لَمَّا تَسَلَّمَ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ مِنَ الْبَدَوِيِّ وَمَضَى بِهَا إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَأَلْبَسَهَا أَفْخَرَ الْمَلْبُوسِ أَخَذَهَا وَنَزَلَ بِهَا إِلَى السُّوقِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-tājira lammā tasallama Nuzhata al-Zamāni mina al-badawiyyi wa-maḍā bihā ilā manzilihi wa-albasahā afkhara al-malbūsi akhadhahā wa-nazala bihā ilā al-sūqi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate-one, that the merchant, when he took-delivery-of Nuzhat al-Zamān from the Bedouin, and went-off with her to his dwelling, and clothed her in the most-splendid of the clothing, took her and went-down with her to the market,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the merchant had taken Nuzhat al-Zamān over from the Bedouin, brought her to his house and dressed her in the finest clothes, he took her down with him to the market,
sentences.n: لَمَّا "when" has its answer in أَخَذَهَا "he took her", with no linking فَـ, as is usual in this text. تَسَلَّمَ (verb V) is "to receive into one's hands, take delivery of", the word for completing a purchase. أَلْبَسَ (verb IV, "make wear") takes two objects: her (-hā) and the clothing.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَ لَهَا مَصَاغًا مِمَّا طَلَبَتْهُ وَوَضَعَهُ فِى بُقْجَةٍ مِنَ الْأَطْلَسِ وَوَضَعَهَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadha lahā maṣāghan mimmā ṭalabathu wa-waḍaʿahu fī buqjatin mina al-aṭlasi wa-waḍaʿahā bayna yaday Nuzhati al-Zamāni
sentences.l: and got for her jewellery, of-what she asked-for, and put it in a bundle of the satin, and put it between the two hands of Nuzhat al-Zamān,
sentences.i: and bought her jewellery of her own choosing, wrapped it in a bundle of satin and laid it before Nuzhat al-Zamān,
sentences.n: مَصَاغ is wrought gold and silver, jewellery. بُقْجَة (from Turkish bohça) is a wrapping-cloth tied into a bundle. بَيْنَ يَدَيْ, "between the two hands of", means simply "in front of". فِى is printed with a dotless yā; read fī.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهَا هٰذَا كُلُّهُ مِنْ أَجْلِكِ وَلَا أُرِيدُ مِنْكِ إِلَّا إِذَا طَلَعْتُ بِكِ إِلَى السُّلْطَانِ نَائِبِ دِمَشْقَ أَنْ تُعْلِمِيهِ بِالثَّمَنِ الَّذِى اشْتَرَيْتُكِ بِهِ وَإِنْكَانَ قَلِيلًا فِى ظُفْرِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā hādhā kulluhu min ajliki wa-lā urīdu minki illā idhā ṭalaʿtu biki ilā al-sulṭāni nāʾibi Dimashqa an tuʿlimīhi bi-al-thamani alladhī ishtaraytuki bihi wa-inkāna qalīlan fī ẓufriki
sentences.l: and said to her: This, all of it, is for your sake, and I do not want from you, except — when I go-up with you to the sultan, the deputy of Damascus — that you inform him of the price which I bought you for, even-if it was little in your fingernail.
sentences.i: and said to her, "All this is for your sake. I want nothing of you but this: when I bring you up before the sultan, the viceroy of Damascus, tell him the price I paid for you, small as it is beside a single nail of yours."
sentences.n: The sentence is "I want nothing from you except ... that you inform him", with the "when"-clause wedged in between. نَائِبُ دِمَشْقَ, "the deputy of Damascus", is the governor who rules the city for the king of Baghdad; the merchant calls him sultan. وَإِنْكَانَ is printed as one word, وَإِنْ كَانَ "even if it was". The last phrase is uncertain: قَلِيلًا فِى ظُفْرِكِ, "little in your nail", seems to mean that the price was a trifle compared with even a fingernail of hers, a compliment to soften what he is asking.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا وَصَلْتِ إِلَيْهِ وَاشْتَرَاكِ مِنِّي اذْكُرِي لَهُ مَا فَعَلْتُ مَعَكِ وَاطْلُبِي لِي مِنْهُ مَنْشُورًا سُلْطَانِيًّا بِالْوَصِيَّةِ عَلَيَّ لِأَذْهَبَ بِهِ إِلَى وَالِدِهِ صَاحِبِ بَغْدَادَ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَمْنَعَ مَنْ يَأْخُذُ مِنِّي مَكْسًا عَلَى قُمَاشٍ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ مَا أَتَّجِرُ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā waṣalti ilayhi wa-ishtarāki minnī udhkurī lahu mā faʿaltu maʿaki wa-uṭlubī lī minhu manshūran sulṭāniyyan bi-al-waṣiyyati ʿalayya li-adhhaba bihi ilā wālidihi ṣāḥibi Baghdāda ʿUmara bni al-Nuʿmāni li-ajli an yamnaʿa man yaʾkhudhu minnī maksan ʿalā qumāshin aw ghayrihi min jamīʿi mā attajiru fīhi
sentences.l: So when you arrive to him and he buys you from me, mention to him what I did with you, and request for me from him a decree, a sultan's, with the commendation upon me, that I may go with it to his father, the master of Baghdad, ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān, for-the-sake that he prevent whoever takes from me a toll on cloth or other-than-it, of all that I trade in.
sentences.i: "When you come before him and he has bought you from me, tell him how I have treated you, and ask him on my behalf for a royal letter commending me, so that I can take it to his father, ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad, and he may stop anyone from levying a toll on me for cloth or any other of the goods I trade in."
sentences.n: مَنْشُور is an open letter of authority, a patent or decree. بِالْوَصِيَّةِ عَلَيَّ, "with the charge concerning me", is a letter of recommendation: الْوَصِيَّةُ عَلَى someone is commending him to another's care. The shadda on عَلَيَّ is the print's own. مَكْس is a market-toll or customs duty, the thing a travelling merchant most wants to escape. The merchant does not yet know who she is; that is the irony of the next lines.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ كَلَامَهُ بَكَتْ وَانْتَحَبَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat kalāmahu bakat wa-intaḥabat
sentences.l: And when she heard his speech, she wept and sobbed.
sentences.i: When she heard his words she wept and sobbed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا التَّاجِرُ يَاسَيِّدَتِي إِنِّي أَرَاكِ كُلَّمَا ذَكَرْتُ بَغْدَادَ تَدْمَعُ عَيْنَاكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-tājiru yā-sayyidatī innī arāki kullamā dhakartu Baghdāda tadmaʿu ʿaynāki
sentences.l: And the merchant said to her: O my lady, indeed I see you, whenever I mention Baghdad, your two eyes shed-tears.
sentences.i: The merchant said to her, "My lady, I see that whenever I mention Baghdad your eyes fill with tears."
sentences.n: أَرَاكِ ... تَدْمَعُ عَيْنَاكِ is "I see you, your eyes weeping": the object of "see" is followed by a clause describing her. يَاسَيِّدَتِي is printed as one word, يَا سَيِّدَتِي.

sentences.t: أَلَكِ فِيهَا أَحَدٌ تُحِبِّينَهُ
sentences.tr: a-laki fīhā aḥadun tuḥibbīnahu
sentences.l: Is-there to-you in it someone you love?
sentences.i: "Is there someone there whom you love?"
sentences.n: أَ is the question particle, joined to لَكِ "to you, you have". Baghdad (a city, feminine) is the "it" of فِيهَا.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ كَانَ تَاجِرًا أَوْغَيْرَهُ فَأَخْبِرِ ينِي بِهِ فَأَنَا أَعْرِفُ جَمِيعَ مَنْ فِيهَا مِنَ التُّجَّارِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَإِنْ أَرَدْتِ رِسَالَةً أَنَا أُوصِلُهَا إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-in kāna tājiran awghayrahu fa-akhbirīnī bihi fa-anā aʿrifu jamīʿa man fīhā mina al-tujjāri wa-ghayrihim wa-in aradti risālatan anā ūṣiluhā ilayhi
sentences.l: So if he is a merchant or other-than-him, then inform me of him, for I know all who are in it, of the merchants and others-than-them; and if you want a message, I, I-will-deliver it to him.
sentences.i: "If he is a merchant or anyone else, tell me about him, for I know everyone there, merchants and others. If you wish to send a message, I will carry it to him."
sentences.n: The print splits فَأَخْبِرِينِي "then tell me" across a space, فاخبر يني, and joins أَوْ غَيْرَهُ into أَوْغَيْرَهُ; we keep both as printed. In the last clause the answer to "if" has no فَـ: أَنَا أُوصِلُهَا, "I deliver it", plain spoken style.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ مَا لِي مَعْرِفَةٌ بِتَاجِرٍ وَلَاغَيْرِهِ وَإِنَّمَا لِي مَعْرِفَةٌ بِالْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ صَاحِبِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-Allāhi mā lī maʿrifatun bi-tājirin wa-lāghayrihi wa-innamā lī maʿrifatun bi-al-maliki ʿUmara bni al-Nuʿmāni ṣāḥibi Baghdāda
sentences.l: And she said: By God, not to-me an acquaintance with a merchant nor other-than-him; but only to-me an acquaintance with the king ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān, master of Baghdad.
sentences.i: She said, "By God, I know no merchant or anyone else there. The only one I know is King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad."
sentences.n: وَلَاغَيْرِهِ is printed as one word, وَلَا غَيْرِهِ "nor anyone else". She does not say that he is her father, and the merchant takes her to mean that she belonged to his household.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ كَلَامَهَا ضَحِكَ وَفَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي وَصَلْتُ إِلَى مَا أُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru kalāmahā ḍaḥika wa-fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan wa-qāla fī nafsihi wa-Allāhi innī waṣaltu ilā mā urīdu
sentences.l: And when the merchant heard her speech, he laughed and rejoiced a rejoicing, intense, and said in himself: By God, indeed I have arrived at what I want.
sentences.i: When the merchant heard her words he laughed and was overjoyed, and said to himself, "By God, I have got what I wanted."
sentences.n: فَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا is the cognate accusative, "rejoiced a great rejoicing", Arabic's usual way of intensifying a verb.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهَا هَلْ عُرِضْتِ عَلَيْهِ سَابِقًا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahā hal ʿuriḍti ʿalayhi sābiqan
sentences.l: Then he said to her: Were you presented to him previously?
sentences.i: Then he said to her, "Were you shown to him for sale before?"
sentences.n: عُرِضَ عَلَى is "be displayed before, offered to", the term for showing a slave-girl to a prospective buyer. We read the passive, since he assumes she has been on the market.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَابَلْ تَرَبَّيْتُ أَنَا وَبِنْتُهُ فَكُنْتُ عَزِيزَةً عِنْدَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lābal tarabbaytu anā wa-bintuhu fa-kuntu ʿazīzatan ʿindahu
sentences.l: And she said: No, rather I was-brought-up, I and his daughter, and I was dear with him,
sentences.i: She said, "No; I was brought up together with his daughter, and he held me dear,
sentences.n: لَابَلْ is printed as one word, لَا بَلْ "no, rather". تَرَبَّيْتُ أَنَا وَبِنْتُهُ, "I was raised, I and his daughter": the pronoun أَنَا is repeated so that a second subject can be joined to it. Her words are literally true and quietly misleading: she herself is his daughter.

sentences.t: وَلِي عِنْدَهُ حُرْمَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lī ʿindahu ḥurmatun kabīratun
sentences.l: And to-me with-him a great standing.
sentences.i: and I have great standing with him.
sentences.n: This finishes her sentence from the line before: she was raised together with the king's daughter, was dear to him, "and to me with him [is] great ḥurma". حُرْمَة is sanctity, the respect owed to someone, hence the regard and standing she enjoys in his house.

sentences.t: فَإِنْكَانَ غَرَضُكَ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ عُمَرَ بْنَ النُّعْمَانِ يَكْتُبُ لَكَ مَا تُرِيدُ فَأْتِنِي بِدَوَاةٍ وَقِرْطَاسٍ فَإِنِّي أَكْتُبُ لَكَ كِتَابًا
sentences.tr: fa-in-kāna gharaḍuka anna al-malika ʿUmara bna al-Nuʿmāni yaktubu laka mā turīdu fa-ʾtinī bi-dawātin wa-qirṭāsin fa-innī aktubu laka kitāban
sentences.l: So if-was your aim that the king ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān writes for-you what you want, then bring me an inkwell and paper, for I write for-you a letter.
sentences.i: So if what you want is for King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān to write you whatever you wish, bring me an inkwell and paper and I will write you a letter.
sentences.n: The print runs إِنْ "if" and كَانَ "was" together as one word, فانكان; we keep the join. After إِنْ the past tense كَانَ has present or future sense. فَأْتِنِي بِـ is "come to me with", that is "bring me": the verb أَتَى takes بِـ for the thing brought. أَكْتُبُ is the plain present, "I write", used here for what she will do at once.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا دَخَلْتَ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ فَسَلِّمِ الْكِتَابَ مِنْ يَدِكَ إِلَى يَدِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā dakhalta ilā madīnati Baghdāda fa-sallimi al-kitāba min yadika ilā yadi al-maliki ʿUmara bni al-Nuʿmāni
sentences.l: And when you have entered into the city of Baghdad, then hand the letter from your hand to the hand of the king ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān,
sentences.i: When you come into the city of Baghdad, put the letter from your own hand into the hand of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān,
sentences.n: "From your hand to his hand": she wants no go-between. The imperative سَلِّمْ takes a helping kasra, سَلِّمِ, before the article that follows.

sentences.t: وَقُلْ لَهُ إِنَّ جَارِيَتَكَ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ قَدْ طَرَقَتْهَا صُرُوفُ اللَّيَالِي وَالْأَيَّامِ حَتَّى بِيعَتْ مِنْ مَكَانٍ إِلَى مَكَانٍ وَهِيَ تُقْرِئُكَ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: wa-qul lahu inna jāriyataka Nuzhata al-Zamāni qad ṭaraqathā ṣurūfu al-layālī wa-al-ayyāmi ḥattā bīʿat min makānin ilā makānin wa-hiya tuqriʾuka al-salāma
sentences.l: and say to him: Your slave-girl Nuzhat al-Zamān, the turns of the nights and the days have come-knocking-upon her, until she was sold from place to place, and she conveys-to-you the greeting.
sentences.i: and say to him, "Your slave-girl Nuzhat al-Zamān has been struck by the turns of fortune, night after night and day after day, until she was sold from place to place, and she sends you her greetings."
sentences.n: صُرُوف, the "turns" or changes, of the nights and days is a stock phrase for the blows of fate. طَرَقَ is to knock at a door, and especially to come by night, as trouble does. أَقْرَأَهُ السَّلَامَ, literally "to make someone read the greeting", is the fixed idiom for sending greetings. Note the irony: "your slave-girl" is the humble form she wants the merchant to use, but the reader knows she is the king's own daughter.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عَنِّي فَأَخْبِرْهُ أَنِّي عِنْدَ نَائِبِ دِمَشْقَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā saʾalaka ʿannī fa-akhbirhu annī ʿinda nāʾibi Dimashqa
sentences.l: And when he asks you about me, then inform him that I am with the deputy of Damascus.
sentences.i: And if he asks you about me, tell him that I am with the governor of Damascus.
sentences.n: نَائِب, "deputy", is the ruler's lieutenant who governs a province in his name; we translate "governor". She speaks as if the sale to the governor were already settled.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ التَّاجِرُ مِنْ فَصَاحَتِهَا وَازْدَادَتْ عِنْدَهُ مَحَبَّتُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-tājiru min faṣāḥatihā wa-izdādat ʿindahu maḥabbatuhā
sentences.l: And the merchant marvelled at her eloquence, and the love of her increased with him.
sentences.i: The merchant marvelled at her eloquence, and his love for her grew.
sentences.n: مَحَبَّتُهَا, "her love", is the love felt for her, not by her: the pronoun stands for the one loved. اِزْدَادَ is the form VIII of زَادَ "increase", with the t of that form turned to d after z.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ مَا أَظُنُّ إِلَّا أَنَّ الرِّجَالَ لَعِبُوا بِعَقْلِكِ وَبَاعُوكِ بِالْمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla mā aẓunnu illā anna al-rijāla laʿibū bi-ʿaqliki wa-bāʿūki bi-al-māli
sentences.l: And he said: I do not think except that the men played with your mind and sold you for the money.
sentences.i: And he said, "I can only suppose that men tricked you and sold you for money."
sentences.n: مَا ... إِلَّا, "not ... except", is the usual way to say "only". لَعِبَ بِعَقْلِهِ, "to play with someone's mind", means to trick or beguile them. In بِالْمَالِ the بِـ is the price, "for money".

sentences.t: فَهَلْ تَحْفَظِينَ الْقُرْآنَ
sentences.tr: fa-hal taḥfaẓīna al-Qurʾāna
sentences.l: So do you keep the Qurʾān?
sentences.i: Do you know the Qurʾān by heart?
sentences.n: حَفِظَ is to keep or guard, and with a text, to have it by heart.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ نَعَمْ وَأَعْرِفُ الْحِكْمَةَ وَالطِّبَّ وَمُقَدِّمَةَ الْمَعْرِفَةِ وَشَرْحَ فُصُولِ بُقْرَاطَ لِجَالِينُوسَ الْحَكِيمِ وَشَرَحْتُهُ أَيْضًا
sentences.tr: qālat naʿam wa-aʿrifu al-ḥikmata wa-al-ṭibba wa-Muqaddimata al-Maʿrifati wa-Sharḥa Fuṣūli Buqrāṭa li-Jālīnūsa al-ḥakīmi wa-sharaḥtuhu ayḍan
sentences.l: She said: Yes, and I know the wisdom and the medicine, and the Introduction of the Knowledge, and the Commentary on the Sections of Hippocrates by Galen the sage, and I commented-on it also.
sentences.i: She said, "Yes. And I know philosophy and medicine, and the Prognostic, and Galen the Sage's Commentary on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, and I have written a commentary on that too.
sentences.n: Here begins her list of what she has studied, mostly the standard books of medieval medicine. الْحِكْمَة is "wisdom", meaning philosophy and the natural sciences. مُقَدِّمَةُ الْمَعْرِفَةِ, "the Introduction of Knowledge", is almost certainly Hippocrates' Prognostic, known in Arabic as تَقْدِمَةُ الْمَعْرِفَةِ, "Foreknowledge"; the print has a slightly different word. The فُصُول, "sections", of Hippocrates (بُقْرَاط) are his Aphorisms, and Galen (جَالِينُوس) wrote a famous commentary on them. In لِجَالِينُوسَ the لِـ marks the author, "by Galen". Both names are foreign and so diptote.

sentences.t: وَقَرَأْتُ التَّذْكِرَةَ وَشَرَحْتُ الْبُرْهَانَ وَطَالَعْتُ مُفْرَدَاتِ ابْنِ الْبَيْطَارِ وَتَكَلَّمْتُ عَلَى الْقَانُونِ الْمَكِّيِّ لِابْنِ سِينَا
sentences.tr: wa-qaraʾtu al-Tadhkirata wa-sharaḥtu al-Burhāna wa-ṭālaʿtu Mufradāti Ibni al-Bayṭāri wa-takallamtu ʿalā al-Qānūni al-Makkiyyi li-Ibni Sīnā
sentences.l: And I read the Tadhkira, and commented-on the Burhān, and studied the Simples of Ibn al-Bayṭār, and spoke upon the Meccan Canon of Ibn Sīnā,
sentences.i: I have read the Tadhkira, written a commentary on the Burhān, studied Ibn al-Bayṭār's Simples, and lectured on the Meccan Canon of Avicenna;
sentences.n: التَّذْكِرَة, "the Memorandum", is probably the great medical handbook of Dāwūd al-Anṭākī (died 1599), widely read in the period when this version of the Nights took shape; other works bear the same title. الْبُرْهَان, "the Proof", cannot be identified with certainty: several books carry the name. The مُفْرَدَات, "simples", of Ibn al-Bayṭār (died 1248) is his dictionary of single drugs. الْقَانُونُ is Avicenna's Canon of Medicine. The print calls it الْمَكِّيّ, "the Meccan", which fits no known title; it may be a slip for الْمَلَكِيّ, "the Royal", the name of another famous textbook, the Royal Book of ʿAlī ibn al-ʿAbbās al-Majūsī, so that the two books have run together. We keep the print's word. تَكَلَّمَ عَلَى, "to speak upon", is to lecture or write on a text.

sentences.t: وَحَلَّيْتُ الرُّمُوزَ وَوَضَعْتُ الْأَشْكَالَ وَتَحَدَّثْتُ فِى الْهَنْدَسَةِ وَأَتْقَنْتُ حِكْمَةَ الْأَبْدَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥallaytu al-rumūza wa-waḍaʿtu al-ashkāla wa-taḥaddathtu fī al-handasati wa-atqantu ḥikmata al-abdāni
sentences.l: and I solved the riddles, and set-down the figures, and discoursed in the geometry, and mastered the wisdom of the bodies;
sentences.i: I have solved riddles and drawn up the figures, discoursed on geometry and mastered the science of the body;
sentences.n: حَلَّيْتُ is a spoken-style form of حَلَلْتُ "I solved": verbs with a doubled root letter are treated like verbs ending in -y, as in colloquial ḥallēt. الرُّمُوز are riddles or cipher-signs. الْأَشْكَال are "figures", most likely geometric figures and proofs, given the geometry that follows; the word also means difficult questions. حِكْمَةُ الْأَبْدَانِ, "the wisdom of bodies", is a name for medicine or physiology. The print writes فِى with a dotless yā.

sentences.t: وَقَرَأْتُ كُتُبَ الشَّافِعِيَّةِ وَقَرَأْتُ الْحَدِيثَ وَالنَّحْوَ وَنَاظَرْتُ الْعُلَمَاءَ
sentences.tr: wa-qaraʾtu kutuba al-Shāfiʿiyyati wa-qaraʾtu al-ḥadītha wa-al-naḥwa wa-nāẓartu al-ʿulamāʾa
sentences.l: and I read the books of the Shāfiʿites, and I read the Ḥadīth and the grammar, and I disputed-with the scholars,
sentences.i: I have read the books of the Shāfiʿī school, studied Ḥadīth and grammar, and held disputations with the learned,
sentences.n: الشَّافِعِيَّة are the followers of the Shāfiʿī school of law, one of the four Sunni schools. الْحَدِيث is the body of reports of the Prophet's sayings and deeds. نَاظَرَ, form III, is to debate someone in formal disputation.

sentences.t: وَتَكَلَّمْتُ فِي سَائِرِ الْعُلُومِ وَأَلَّفْتُ فِي عِلْمِ الْمَنْطِقِ وَالْبَيَانِ وَالْحِسَابِ وَالْجَدَاوِلِ
sentences.tr: wa-takallamtu fī sāʾiri al-ʿulūmi wa-allaftu fī ʿilmi al-manṭiqi wa-al-bayāni wa-al-ḥisābi wa-al-jadāwili
sentences.l: and I spoke in all the sciences, and composed in the science of the logic, and the rhetoric, and the arithmetic, and the tables;
sentences.i: I have spoken on every science, and written books on logic, rhetoric, arithmetic and the astronomical tables.
sentences.n: سَائِر here means "all" (strictly "the rest"). أَلَّفَ, form II, is to compose a book. الْبَيَان is the part of rhetoric that treats figurative speech. الْجَدَاوِل, "tables", are most likely the astronomical tables used for reckoning the stars and the calendar.

sentences.t: وَأَعْرِفُ الرُّوحَانِيَّ وَالْمِيقَاتَ وَفَهِمْتُ هٰذِهِ الْعُلُومَ كُلَّهَا
sentences.tr: wa-aʿrifu al-rūḥāniyya wa-al-mīqāta wa-fahimtu hādhihi al-ʿulūma kullahā
sentences.l: And I know the spiritual and the timekeeping, and I understood these sciences, all of them.
sentences.i: I know the science of spirits and the science of timekeeping, and I have understood all of these sciences."
sentences.n: الرُّوحَانِيّ, "the spiritual", is the science of spirits: the magic of letters and names used to summon or bind spirits and jinn. الْمِيقَات is the astronomical science of fixing times, above all the hours of prayer.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلتَّاجِرِ ائْتِنِي بِدَوَاةٍ وَقِرْطَاسٍ حَتَّى أَكْتُبَ لَكَ كِتَابًا يَنْفَعُكَ فِي سَفَرِكَ إِلَى الْبِلَادِ وَيُغْنِيكَ عَنْ مُجَلَّدَاتِ الْأَسْفَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-tājiri iʾtinī bi-dawātin wa-qirṭāsin ḥattā aktuba laka kitāban yanfaʿuka fī safarika ilā al-bilādi wa-yughnīka ʿan mujalladāti al-asfāri
sentences.l: Then she said to the merchant: Bring me an inkwell and paper, so that I write for-you a writing that profits you in your journey to the lands and makes-you-free-of the bound-volumes of the tomes.
sentences.i: Then she said to the merchant, "Bring me an inkwell and paper, so that I can write you something that will serve you on your journey to those lands and spare you whole bound volumes of books."
sentences.n: There is a play on words: سَفَر is "journey" and أَسْفَار, the plural of سِفْر, are "tomes", the same letters. أَغْنَاهُ عَنْ, "to make one free of need for", is "to spare". After حَتَّى "so that" the verb أَكْتُبَ is subjunctive.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ ذٰلِكَ مِنْهَا صَاحَ بَخٍ بَخٍ فَيَا سَعْدَ مَنْ تَكُونِينَ فِي قَصْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru dhālika minhā ṣāḥa bakhin bakhin fa-yā saʿda man takūnīna fī qaṣrihi
sentences.l: And when the merchant heard that from her, he cried: Bravo, bravo! And O the fortune of him whom you will be in his palace!
sentences.i: When the merchant heard this from her, he cried out, "Bravo, bravo! Happy the man in whose palace you will live!"
sentences.n: بَخٍ بَخٍ is an old exclamation of admiration, "excellent!". In يَا سَعْدَ مَنْ ..., "O the good fortune of him who ...", the يَا is an exclamation rather than a call. مَنْ تَكُونِينَ فِي قَصْرِهِ is "he whom you will be in his palace": the pronoun -hi at the end points back to مَنْ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنَاهَا بِدَوَاةٍ وَقِرْطَاسٍ وَقَلَمٍ مِنْ نُحَاسٍ
sentences.tr: thumma anāhā bi-dawātin wa-qirṭāsin wa-qalamin min nuḥāsin
sentences.l: Then he came-to-her with an inkwell and paper and a pen of brass.
sentences.i: Then he brought her an inkwell, paper and a brass pen.
sentences.n: The print has اناها, which is no word. It is almost certainly a misprint for اتاها, أَتَاهَا "he came to her", the two letters differing by a single dot; with بِـ that verb means "bring", as at the start of this passage. We keep the printed letters and translate as أَتَاهَا. The pen is a reed-shaped pen of brass.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَحْضَرَ التَّاجِرُ ذٰلِكَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا بَاسَ الْأَرْضَ تَعْظِيمًا لَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aḥḍara al-tājiru dhālika bayna yadayhā bāsa al-arḍa taʿẓīman lahā
sentences.l: And when the merchant had brought that between her two hands, he kissed the ground in honouring of her.
sentences.i: When the merchant had set these things before her, he kissed the ground in reverence to her.
sentences.n: بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا, "between her two hands", is "before her". بَاسَ is the spoken-style verb "to kiss", for Classical قَبَّلَ; kissing the ground is the gesture one makes before a ruler. تَعْظِيمًا is an accusative of purpose, "out of reverence".

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ الدَّرْجَ وَتَنَاوَلَتِ الْقَلَمَ وَكَتَبَتْ فِيهِ شِعْ—رًا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhat Nuzhatu al-Zamāni al-darja wa-tanāwalati al-qalama wa-katabat fīhi shiʿran
sentences.l: And Nuzhat al-Zamān took the scroll, and took-up the pen, and wrote in it verse:
sentences.i: Nuzhat al-Zamān took the scroll, picked up the pen, and wrote these verses on it:
sentences.n: The print breaks شِعْرًا "verse" across a line with a dash, شع—را; we keep the dash as printed, and the word is read as one, shiʿran. الدَّرْج is a roll of paper, a scroll. The poem follows.

sentences.t:
اَرَى النَّوْمَ مِنْ عَيْنِيَّ قَدْ نَفَرَا * أَاَنْتَ عَلَّمْتَ طَرْفِي بَعْدَكَ السَّهَرَا
وَمَالِذِكْرِكَ يُصْلِي النَّارَ فِي كَبِدِي * اَهَكَذَا كُلُّ صَبٍّ الْمَهْوَى ذَكَرَا
سَقْيًا لَا يَّامِنَا مَا كَانَ اَطْيَبَهَا * وَلَّتْ وَلَمْ اَقْضِ مِنْ لَذَّاتِهَا وَطَرَا
اَسْتَعْطِفُ الرِّيحَ اَنَّ الرِّيحَ حَامِلَةٌ * اِلَى الْمُتَيَّمِ مِنْ اَكْنَافِكُمْ خَبَرَا
يَشْكُو اِلَيْكَ مُحِبٌّ قَلَّ نَاصِرُهُ * وَلِلْفِرَاقِ خُطُوبٌ تَصْدَعُ الْحَجَرَا
sentences.tr:
arā al-nawma min ʿayniyya qad nafarā * a-anta ʿallamta ṭarfī baʿdaka al-saharā
wa-mā li-dhikrika yuṣlī al-nāra fī kabidī * a-hākadhā kullu ṣabbin al-mahwā dhakarā
saqyan la-yyāminā mā kāna aṭyabahā * wallat wa-lam aqḍi min ladhdhātihā waṭarā
astaʿṭifu al-rīḥa anna al-rīḥa ḥāmilatun * ilā al-mutayyami min aknāfikum khabarā
yashkū ilayka muḥibbun qalla nāṣiruhu * wa-li-al-firāqi khuṭūbun taṣdaʿu al-ḥajarā
sentences.l:
I see sleep, from my eyes, has fled; * is-it you who taught my glance, after you, the wakefulness?
And what is-it with remembrance-of-you, that it roasts the fire in my liver? * Is thus every passion-sick-one who remembered the place-of-love?
A watering for our days — how sweet they were! * They turned-away, and I did not fulfil of their pleasures a desire.
I beg-the-kindness-of the wind, for the wind is a carrier * to the love-enslaved-one, from your sides, of news.
There complains to you a lover few-are his helpers; * and parting has calamities that split the stone.
sentences.i:
I see that sleep has fled my eyes: was it you who taught my glance to wake after you were gone?
Why is it that the thought of you sets fire to my very liver? Is every lovesick man like this, who calls the beloved place to mind?
May rain water the days we had, and how sweet they were! They turned away before I had my fill of their delights.
I plead with the wind to be kind, for the wind can carry news from your country to the one enslaved by love.
A lover with few to help him makes his complaint to you; and parting brings disasters that would split a stone.
sentences.n: Every word of these lines is pointed in the print, and the points are copied as they stand. The print joins وَمَالِذِكْرِكَ into one word: read وَمَا لِذِكْرِكَ, "and what is it with remembrance of you". It splits لَا يَّامِنَا: this is "for our days", normally لِأَيَّامِنَا, but the print puts a fatḥa on the lām and leaves a gap; we keep that and transliterate it as printed. عَيْنِيَّ "my eyes" has a kasra where the dual "my two eyes" would have a fatḥa (ʿaynayya). In اَنَّ الرِّيحَ the print has anna, though after "I plead with the wind" one expects inna, "for the wind ...". The end of the second line, كُلُّ صَبٍّ الْمَهْوَى ذَكَرَا, is unclear: we take الْمَهْوَى as "the place (or object) of love" and the object of ذَكَرَا, "every lover who remembered his beloved", but the article on a word inside the phrase is odd and something may have dropped out. سَقْيًا "a watering!" is the old blessing on a place or time: may rain fall on it. The rhyme is -arā throughout.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا لَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ كِتَابَةِ شِعْرِهَا كَتَبَتْ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ وَهِيَ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā lammā faraghat min kitābati shiʿrihā katabat baʿda dhālika hādhā al-kalāma wa-hiya taqūlu
sentences.l: Then she, when she finished from the writing of her poetry, wrote after that these words, and she was saying:
sentences.i: When she had finished writing out her poem, she wrote these words after it:
sentences.n: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا "then she" is the storyteller's way of moving on; إِنَّ simply carries the pronoun. وَهِيَ تَقُولُ "and she saying" introduces what she writes, as if she spoke it.

sentences.t: مَنِ اخْتَرَمَهَا الْفِكْرُ وَأَنْحَلَهَا السَّهَرُ فَظُلْمَتُهَا لَا تَجِدُ لَهَا مِنْ أَنْوَارٍ وَلَا تَعْلَمُ اللَّيْلَ مِنَ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: mani ikhtaramahā al-fikru wa-anḥalahā al-saharu fa-ẓulmatuhā lā tajidu lahā min anwārin wa-lā taʿlamu al-layla mina al-nahāri
sentences.l: [She is] one whom brooding has cut-off and wakefulness has made-thin; so her darkness — she finds not for it any lights, and she knows not the night from the day.
sentences.i: She whom care has consumed and sleeplessness has wasted, whose darkness knows no light, who cannot tell night from day,
sentences.n: The letter is in rhymed prose: al-fikru / al-saharu, anwārin / al-nahāri, and so on through the passage. We read the opening من as مَنْ "she whom", the heading of the writer's self-description; it could also be مِنْ "from", the usual first word of a letter ("from her whom ..."), with the relative left unwritten. اخْتَرَمَ is "to cut off, carry off", used of death taking someone.

sentences.t: وَتَتَقَلَّبُ عَلَى مَرَاقِدِ الْبَيْنِ وَتَكْتَحِلُ بِمَرَاوِدِ الْأَرَقِ وَهِيَ لِلنُّجُومِ رَقِيبَةٌ وَلِلظَّلَامِ نَقِيبَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-tataqallabu ʿalā marāqidi al-bayni wa-taktaḥilu bi-marāwidi al-araqi wa-hiya li-al-nujūmi raqībatun wa-li-al-ẓalāmi naqībatun
sentences.l: and she tosses-about on the beds of separation, and she paints-her-eyes-with-kohl with the kohl-needles of sleeplessness, and she is, to the stars, a watcher, and to the darkness, an overseer;
sentences.i: who tosses on the beds of separation and lines her eyes with the kohl-sticks of wakefulness, who keeps watch on the stars and stands guard over the dark;
sentences.n: A مِرْوَد is the little rod used to put kohl on the eyelids: instead of kohl she puts sleeplessness on her eyes. رَقِيبَةٌ and نَقِيبَةٌ rhyme: "watcher" and "overseer".

sentences.t: قَدْ أَذَا بَهَا الْكُفْرُ وَالنُّحُولُ وَشَرْحُ حَالِهَا يَطُولُ لَا مُسَاعِدَ لَهَا غَيْرُ الْعَبَرَاتِ
sentences.tr: qad adhā-bahā al-kufru wa-al-nuḥūlu wa-sharḥu ḥālihā yaṭūlu lā musāʿida lahā ghayru al-ʿabarāti
sentences.l: indeed there have melted her the unbelief [?] and the wasting, and the explaining of her state is long; no helper is there for her other than the tears.
sentences.i: who has been melted away by care and wasting, whose state would take long to tell, and who has no one to help her but her tears.
sentences.n: The print splits one word in two: اذا بها is أَذَابَهَا "(they) have melted her", from أَذَابَ "to melt", and we point the two printed halves so that together they read adhābahā (the verb is singular before its subjects, as usual). الْكُفْرُ, as printed, means "unbelief", which makes poor sense here; it is very likely a misprint, perhaps for الْفِكْرُ "brooding" (the same letters reordered, and the word that opened the letter) or for الْكَمَدُ "grief". The literal layer gives the printed word; the idiomatic follows the likely sense. النُّحُولُ "wasting" rhymes with يَطُولُ.

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْ—يَ—اتَ
sentences.tr: wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And she recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: And she recited these verses:
sentences.n: The print splits الابيات with two dashes, الاب—ي—ات; we keep them as printed and read the word as الْأَبْيَاتَ, "the verses", the object of "saying".

sentences.t:
مَا غَرَّدَتْ سَحَرًا وَرْقَاءُ فِي فَنَنٍ * اِلَّا تَحَرَّكَ عِنْدِي قَاتِلُ الشَّجَنِ
وَلَا تَأَوَّهَ مُشْتَاقٌ بِهِ طَرَبٌ * اِلَى الْاَحِبَّةِ اِلَّا زَادَ بِي حَزَنِي
اَشْكُو الْغَرَامَ اِلَى مَنْ لَيْسَ يَرْحَمُنِي * كَمْ فَرَّقَ الْوَجْدُ بَيْنَ الرُّوحِ وَالْبَدَنِ
sentences.tr:
mā gharradat saḥaran warqāʾu fī fananin * illā taḥarraka ʿindī qātilu al-shajani
wa-lā taʾawwaha mushtāqun bihi ṭarabun * ilā al-aḥibbati illā zāda bī ḥazanī
ashkū al-gharāma ilā man laysa yarḥamunī * kam farraqa al-wajdu bayna al-rūḥi wa-al-badani
sentences.n: These lines too are pointed in the print and copied as they stand. The pattern مَا ... إِلَّا "not ... but" means "never ... without": every time the dove sings, the grief stirs. قَاتِلُ الشَّجَنِ "the killer of grief" is the grief that kills (a noun-plus-genitive used as a description), not something that kills grief. وَرْقَاءُ is the ash-grey dove, the bird of lament in Arabic poetry. The rhyme is -ani / -anī.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَفَاضَتْ دُمُوعَ الْعَيْنِ وَكَتَبَتْ أَيْضًا هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma afāḍat dumūʿa al-ʿayni wa-katabat ayḍan hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then she poured-forth the tears of the eye, and she wrote also these two verse-lines:
sentences.i: Then she shed tears from her eyes and wrote these two lines as well:

sentences.t:
اَبْلَى الْهَوَى اَسَفًا يَوْمَ النَّوَى بَدَنِي * وَفَرَّقَ الْهَجْرُ بَيْنَ الْجَفْنِ وَالْوَسَنِ
كَفَى بِجِسْمِي نُحُولًا اِنَّنِي رَجُلٌ * لَوْلَا مُخَاطَبَتِي اِيَّاكَ لَمْ تَرَنِي
sentences.tr:
ablā al-hawā asafan yawma al-nawā badanī * wa-farraqa al-hajru bayna al-jafni wa-al-wasani
kafā bi-jismī nuḥūlan innanī rajulun * lawlā mukhāṭabatī iyyāka lam tarani
sentences.l:
Wore-out love, in grief, on the day of distance, my body; * and parted the forsaking between the eyelid and the sleep.
Enough for my body as thinness that-I am a man * — were-it-not-for my addressing you, you would not see me.
sentences.i:
On the day of parting, love has worn my body down with grief, and abandonment has parted my eyelids from sleep.
I am so wasted it is enough to say I am a man you would not even see, were I not speaking to you.
sentences.n: The second line is a famous verse of al-Mutanabbī, quoted here as it stood, with its masculine رَجُلٌ "a man", though a woman is writing it. The print points اِنَّنِي with a kasra; after كَفَى "it is enough that ..." the grammar asks for أَنَّنِي (annanī), and we transliterate the vowel as printed. In كَفَى بِجِسْمِي نُحُولًا the accusative نُحُولًا says in what respect it is enough: "as for thinness". تَرَنِي is jussive after لَمْ, so the long ā of تَرَى drops: "you would not see me". The rhyme -ani / -anī matches the poem before.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أفَاضَتْ دُمُوعَ الْعَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma afāḍat dumūʿa al-ʿayni
sentences.l: Then she-made-flow the-tears-of the eye.
sentences.i: Then the tears poured from her eyes,
sentences.n: اَفَاضَ (form IV of فَاضَ "overflow") is transitive, "make overflow, pour forth", so دُمُوعَ is its object: she let the tears of the eye run. "The eye" is singular and generic, as often in this phrase.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ كَتَبَتْ فِي أسْفَلِ الدَّرْجِ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika katabat fī asfali al-darji hādhā
sentences.l: And after that she-wrote in the-lowest-part-of the scroll this:
sentences.i: and after that she wrote this at the foot of the scroll:
sentences.n: الدَّرْج is a roll or scroll of paper, the letter she has just filled with verse. هٰذَا points forward to the signature that follows; اَسْفَل, the elative "lowest", is used here as a noun, "the bottom".

sentences.t: مِنْ عِنْدِ الْبَعِيدَةِ عَنِ الْأهْلِ وَالْأوْطَانِ الْحَزِينَةِ الْقَلْبِ وَالْجَنَانِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: min ʿindi al-baʿīdati ʿani al-ahli wa-al-awṭāni al-ḥazīnati al-qalbi wa-al-janāni Nuzhati al-Zamāni
sentences.l: From the-presence-of the far-one from the family and the homelands, the sad-of the heart and the soul: Nuzhat al-Zamān.
sentences.i: "From her who is far from her family and her homelands, sad of heart and soul: Nuzhat al-Zamān."
sentences.n: A signature in rhymed prose: al-awṭān, al-janān, al-Zamān. مِنْ عِنْدِ is the letter-writer's "from". الْحَزِينَةِ الْقَلْبِ is an adjective with a following noun that specifies it, "sad as to the heart", the Arabic way of saying "sad-hearted". جَنَان is the heart or inward soul, paired with قَلْب for the rhyme. Her name stands in apposition and so takes the genitive with the rest.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَفَّتِ الدَّرْجَ وَنَاوَلَتْهُ لِلتَّاجِرِ
sentences.tr: thumma laffati al-darja wa-nāwalathu li-al-tājiri
sentences.l: Then she-rolled-up the scroll and she-handed-it to-the merchant.
sentences.i: Then she rolled up the scroll and handed it to the merchant,
sentences.n: لَفَّتِ takes a helping kasra before the article. Classical نَاوَلَ takes two direct objects ("hand someone something"); here the receiver is marked with لِـ, a looser usage you will meet often in this text.

sentences.t: فَأخَذَهُ وَقَبَّلَهُ وَعَرَفَ مَا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahu wa-qabbalahu wa-ʿarafa mā fīhi
sentences.l: And-he-took-it and kissed-it and knew what in-it.
sentences.i: and he took it, kissed it, and understood what was in it.
sentences.n: مَا فِيهِ is "what [is] in it", a relative clause with no verb.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ وَقَالَ سُبْحَانَ مَنْ صَوَّرَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa wa-qāla subḥāna man ṣawwaraki
sentences.l: And-he-rejoiced and said: Glory-to who formed-you!
sentences.i: He was glad and said, "Glory be to Him who fashioned you!"
sentences.n: The print itself marks the shadda of صوّرك. صَوَّرَ (form II) is "to form, give shape to"; praising the One who "fashioned" someone is a stock exclamation at beauty, here at her skill with words as well. The ending -ki is our reading: he addresses her.

sentences.t: وَأدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَ—احِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-muba—āḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The print splits the last word with a dash, المب—اح, and we keep it as printed; read al-mubāḥ. This is the stock close of a night: morning overtakes Shahrazād and she stops "the permitted speech", the story she was allowed to tell. شَهْرَزَادَ is the object, الصَّبَاحُ the subject placed after it.
